title: OAuth 2.0: roles and flows
summary: Why OAuth exists, who the four parties are, how the authorization code flow works, and why the implicit and password grants are gone.

steps.title: Don't give apps your password
body: A printing service wants to read photos from your cloud drive. The bad old way: give it your cloud password. Now it can do *everything* you can, forever, and the only way to stop it is to change your password everywhere.

**OAuth 2.0** (RFC 6749) is the standard fix: **delegated authorization**. You approve a *limited* grant ("read photos") at the cloud provider, and the app receives an **access token** for exactly that, which you can revoke on its own. The app never sees your password.
The four roles:
| Role | Who | In the example |
| **Resource owner** | the user who can grant access | you |
| **Client** | the application that wants access | the printing service |
| **Authorization server** | issues tokens after authenticating the user and getting consent | the cloud provider's login service |
| **Resource server** | the API that holds the data and accepts tokens | the cloud photo API |
In your own systems the authorization server is often Entra ID, Auth0, Okta or Keycloak, and the resource servers are your APIs.

steps.prompt: A company uses Entra ID to let its React app call its Orders API for a signed-in employee. Match each role.

steps.title: The authorization code flow
body: The main flow for anything a user signs in to:
```text
1. Client redirects the browser to the authorization server:
GET https://login.example.com/authorize
?response_type=code
&client_id=photo-printer
&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fprinter.example%2Fcallback
&scope=photos.read
&state=x7Gq2...                  (random, remembered by the client)
&code_challenge=p2dtQq...&code_challenge_method=S256   (PKCE, next lesson)
2. The user logs in there (password, MFA...) and approves the scopes.
3. The authorization server redirects back with a short-lived, single-use code:
GET https://printer.example/callback?code=SplxlOBeZQ&state=x7Gq2...
4. The client checks state, then swaps the code for tokens, server to server:
POST https://login.example.com/token
grant_type=authorization_code&code=SplxlOBeZQ&redirect_uri=...&client_id=...&code_verifier=...
5. Response:
{ "access_token": "eyJ...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600,
"refresh_token": "8xLOxBtZp8", "scope": "photos.read" }
6. Client calls the API:  Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
The browser only ever carries the **code**, and the code is useless without the second step.

lines: the client redirects the browser to /authorize with client_id, scope, state and a code challenge
the user signs in at the authorization server and consents
the authorization server redirects to the redirect_uri with a code and the state
the client checks the state matches the one it sent
the client posts the code and code verifier to /token
the client calls the API with the access token

steps.title: state, redirect_uri, and what is gone
body: - **`state`**: a random value the client stores before redirecting and checks on the way back. Without it an attacker can make your browser complete *their* login (CSRF on the callback), so you end up using the attacker's account.
- **`redirect_uri`**: the authorization server only redirects to URIs **pre-registered exactly** for that client. Loose matching (prefixes, wildcards) has leaked countless codes to attacker pages.
**Gone in OAuth 2.1 and the current Security BCP (RFC 9700):**

- **Implicit flow** (`response_type=token`): the access token came back directly in the URL fragment. It leaked through browser history, `Referer` headers and extensions, couldn't be bound to the client, and had no refresh. Browser apps now use the code flow with PKCE instead.
- **Resource owner password grant** (`grant_type=password`): the client collects the user's password, exactly what OAuth was invented to avoid, and it can't support MFA or federated login.
Still current: **authorization code + PKCE** (users), **client credentials** (service to service), **refresh token**, and the **device code** flow for TVs and CLIs.

steps.prompt: Why was the implicit flow deprecated?
options: It put the access token in the browser's URL, where history, logs and Referer headers could leak it, with no way to bind it to the client
It was too slow because it needed two round trips
It required a client secret in JavaScript
steps.explain: The code flow keeps the token out of the URL entirely; PKCE makes even a stolen code useless.

steps.prompt: Query string values must be percent-encoded. What does this print?
steps.explain: Scopes are separated by spaces, which become `%20`. A redirect URI is itself a URL and must be fully escaped to travel as one parameter.

steps.title: Build the authorize URL
prompt: Write `string BuildAuthorizeUrl(string authority, string clientId, string redirectUri, string[] scopes, string state, string codeChallenge)` that returns
- Every value escaped with `Uri.EscapeDataString`; scopes joined with a single space first.
- A trailing `/` on `authority` must not produce `//authorize`.
